messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mereana is a 66-year-old widow who has worked for years as a network engineer, a role that once suited her pleasure in orderly systems and solvable problems. The assault happened late one evening after a client dinner. A male colleague she had trusted walked her to her car and, reeking of whiskey, insisted on hugging her when she thanked him for the ride to the parking garage. When she stiffened and tried to pull away, he held on, pressed himself against her, and overpowered her. What has stayed with her is not only the force of his hands but the sequence of small betrayals: the smell of alcohol on his breath, the way an ordinary gesture of affection turned dangerous, and the sickening fact that someone she knew well enough to stand close to became the person who violated her body. In the weeks after, she had come to believe that she could not stop bad things from happening once another person decided to cross a line. She was equally tormented by the sense that in freezing and trying to placate him she had acted against the woman she understood herself to be—competent, firm, not someone who yielded. She spoke of her body with shame, as if it had become marked by what was done to it.

Those beliefs changed what stood out to her in daily life. Hugs in church, a neighbor reaching warmly for her shoulder, even a coworker leaning in with unusual friendliness all began to feel loaded before anything happened. Emotional closeness itself started to seem like the beginning of danger, because she was certain she had once mistaken closeness for safety and had been proven catastrophically wrong. The smell of alcohol became especially potent; if someone passed her in the office hallway after lunch smelling faintly of liquor, she felt her stomach drop before she had fully registered why. What frightened her most was how quickly her mind translated these moments into the same conclusion: this is how it starts, and I will not be able to stop it.

Her response was to narrow her life in ways that felt sensible to her at the time. She stopped hugging relatives and began stepping back from friends who wanted to talk intimately about her grief, her loneliness, or the assault. At work she kept interactions clipped and technical, avoiding the softer conversations that had once made her feel part of a team. When a younger colleague put a hand lightly on her arm while thanking her for solving a server outage, Mereana jerked so sharply that the woman apologized, bewildered; after that, Mereana took pains to stand where no one could approach her from behind and kept a rigid physical distance. She gave up dinners out, gardening club, and the Saturday ukulele group she had once enjoyed, telling herself she was too tired. She also began controlling food with increasing strictness, measuring and limiting what she ate because the sensation of discipline gave her a thin, temporary sense of command over a body that otherwise felt exposed and unreliable.

Her days became organized around scanning. In conference rooms she immediately noted the heavy stapler, the letter opener, the metal water bottle on the table; in elevators she tracked who stood closest and where the emergency button was. Unexpected touch made her whole body flare into alarm. Even when people reassured her—when her sister said she was safe at home, when HR assured her the colleague no longer worked there—she found she could not believe them in any lasting way. From that constant watchfulness, her avoiding made even more sense to her: if danger could come from ordinary warmth, from someone moving close, from not seeing what was in another person’s hand, then refusing intimacy, shrinking pleasure, and controlling food felt like practical precautions rather than symptoms.

Yet those habits deepened the very convictions that tormented her. Each declined invitation and each retreat from affection left her more alone with the idea that closeness was incompatible with safety. The more she treated her body as something to manage strictly and keep inaccessible, the more ashamed she felt of it, as though its only meanings were vulnerability and contamination. She took no satisfaction in the control she exercised; instead it seemed to confirm her helplessness, because such elaborate rules were, in her mind, only necessary for someone fundamentally unprotected. As months turned into years, the world of triggers expanded. Because she had so consistently pulled away from hugs and emotional warmth, even benign gestures now arrived already charged, and the smell of alcohol in a grocery line or on a technician visiting her office could ruin the rest of her day.

By the time she sought treatment, the cost had become unmistakable. A close friend tried to embrace her after a memorial service for another widow in their church, and Mereana recoiled so hard she nearly fell, then went home and skipped dinner as if punishing herself. At work she remained competent, but younger staff had begun describing her as intimidating and unreachable, and she privately feared retirement because she could see how empty her life had become. She came in saying she was tired of arranging every room, every meal, and every relationship around the possibility of being overpowered again. What she is most afraid of is that this is permanent—that any affection, any closeness, will always feel like the first second of another assault. What she is hoping, though she says it cautiously, is that she might someday be able to believe safety when it is there and inhabit her own body without shame.
